title: Stages of Monastic Life
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from Zoketsu Norman Fischer's essay "Stages of Monastic Practice," collected in When You Greet Me I Bow, and adds a personal sketch of its eight stages. Memories of Norman come first: a 1986 Rohatsu sesshin at Green Gulch, where Norman answered complaints about straining with "isn't breathing wonderful?", and the years Norman flew north to teach small groups in Bellingham and Vancouver. The stages run from the honeymoon, disappointment and betrayal, and exploration of commitment through commitment and flight, the dry place, gratitude, love, and letting go. Nomon illustrates commitment and flight with a sangha member who left for years, returned, and left again. The essay's passage on love closes at a graveside, where the person being buried is Buddha.

And then doing various ritual steps of training, you know, sort of ritualize and clarify that that's going on, ordinations and so on.

No, no, he said, "I'm really sorry that this happened to you."

So anyway, we do have teachers and students, but we hold it lightly as the short answer.
Never feeling like, you know, anybody owns anybody.
I'm really resistant to the personal, the possessive pronoun that gets used in some places.
"She's my student," "he's my student."

And I've known Norman a long time.
I first met him at Green Gulch's Farm Zen Center in California in the fall of 1986.
I visited there for the first time for a week the previous spring, and I had met some people who ended up being important to me and to the Dharma world.

Wonderful teacher.

It was that next fall that I took a year off from college and I signed up for their fall practice period.
And I remember just now that my beloved grandmother, very spiritual grandmother, Fran, paid most of the fee so I could afford it.
Norman was actually assisting with the practice period, which was led by Katagiri Roshi.
We did have a class with Norman on the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 10,000 lines, which has a chapter in it we often chant about the wisdom beyond wisdom.
I had a warm feeling about him but didn't know him that well.

But then the practice period ended with the full eight day or seven and a half day Rohatsu sesshin.

For most people, I think.
A big sesshin with a hundred people in this basement zendo at San Francisco.

And Norman was like across from the, across the aisle from me.

And then figuring the only way through was to try even harder.
And I remember at one point I was like seeing those kind of swimmy things you see when you press your eyelid, except my eyes were open.

My face was a mask of tension and my shoulders were a rack and my knees hurt and la la la, you know.
So Norman, I think like the other senior students who were there, did take turns offering practice discussions.

So I asked to see him.
I told him about all this.

Very kind of stern appearance.

Is that near Bellingham, Washington?"
And I said, "Well, yes, it is right across the border, you know."

And after I'd moved to Bellingham, in one of those trips, I met Florence Caplow at a practice thing.
I met Bob Penny, who's here, through a work thing and eventually started a little practice group, you know.
I said two pivotal things, I think I'll just say one for brevity.

Like what a lot of effort, you know, getting on the plane every other month pretty much to come see us.

That these opportunities to work with these kind of newer, vibrant, small groups were a little bit like what Suzuki Roshi talked about after he came to America.
The sense of beginner's mind, you know, the sense of fresh, new, enthusiastic practice.
And so those years I think were really important and helpful to him too in his own development as a Zen teacher that we helped.
The teacher helped us to grow and we helped the teacher to grow as well.

It's completely mutual.

I thought it'd be useful to bring up this piece, and I don't know if all that introductory stuff was essential or not, but I felt like I wanted to do that too.

Because somehow we're always doing this work; we're always in these stages that he talks about here, and the framework is monastic practice because that's where this stuff was really designed and refined and practiced.

Although Soto Zen is famous for effectively in Japan sort of bringing some sense of Zen practice to ordinary people, farmers, and regular village people, that's only kind of relative to the other school of Zen which stayed completely elite with the samurai warlords in the capital.
Even Soto Zen was still, like most religious institutions, a little bit of an elite thing.

The villagers would maybe come for a special ceremony, and they do actually like kind of a precept ceremony for regular village people and give them the same kind of documents that we give out now, which was a big thing.
But the regular village people didn't come to Zazen as far as I can tell; they were too busy with their lives, and I don't know if they were even welcome.
So this has always been a monastic practice for a few dedicated monks and nuns to really polish and refine and devote themselves to.
Pretty much it's a modern idea, modern here, and also modern in Japan for anybody and everybody to come to Zazen.

Sort of a concentrated way to do what we're doing, but not really that different.
So here's the opening section of Norman's "Stages of Monastic Practice," and then I'll give kind of my version of the stages.
This is Norman: Religious texts make monastic life sound deep and constant, a life that has been the same for a thousand years—timeless and seamless.
Of course, this can't really be true; everything changes.
Traditions aren't eternal; however, slowly they always change even when no one wants them to.

On the other hand, maybe there is the reason we think of monastic life this way—maybe underneath all of us there is another person, a monastic who is living or at any rate appears to live and imagines it's possible to live a true and perfect human life.
I think I might have miscopied a little word there, so maybe within all of us there's a monastic who is aspiring and even actually is some kind of perfect, thoughtful, deep human life.
Norman again: I believe all of us have this monastic in us.
However noisy and excitable we are, I think we all have some place in us a deep longing to live this life of silence and perfection, and what a relief and how beautiful that would be.
When we're completely out of touch with this wish, as most of us usually are, we suffer.
We run around looking for something we can't seem to find, or our lives don't work out.

When we are in touch with it, with this inner monastic, as we are more overtly in retreat, or even in a few meditation practice moments of meditation practice, or on the beach, or alone under the stars, or in the wilderness, we feel whole and we can approach others and the complicated world with a measure of equanimity.

So this monastic life, this way of silence and wholeness, this sacred way, this ideal lives at the bottom of our hearts and is reflected back to us in reverie, in religious experience, and in religious literature.
But ideas, when we mistake them for concrete realities, can be poisonous.
Ideas can be poisonous.
Ideas when we mistake them for concrete realities can be poisonous.
Ideals inspire us to surpass ourselves and to be fully human; we need them, but of course we never do surpass ourselves.
We remain imperfect.
Religious ideals inspire us to keep on trying and failing with sincere good spirit.
The fact that we have so often missed this point accounts, I think, for the sorry history of religion.
In the name of ideals we berate ourselves and others for not measuring up, and we can even kill people to improve their chances of becoming perfect.

The monastic life appears in the text of religious traditions as the ideal way to live: living in perfect obedience, perfect peace, perfect gratitude and silence, and deep meditation in prayer, in harmony and calmness in the quiet mountains among the clouds and the forests, or in the rolling hills under sunny skies.
Maybe it is like this someplace on earth or at least someplace in our imaginations, but in our conscious life it is never this way.
So that's Norman's opening of this essay.
So I really am appreciating this idea which I had forgotten of each of us having this inner monastic within us whom we are often unaware of, but who brings us to practice somehow.
Doesn't that really feel right?
You think about like why do you come to practice, and you can list various practical ideas about why you're doing this, right?
It's interesting, it helps me calm down.
I like the people who are drawn to it; it's good for me.
But those kind of ideas don't really seem to be quite enough really, right?
To explain the depth of commitment that's involved in this thing.

But this idea of the inner monastic gradually making herself known, or the yearning to connect with him, this inner monastic, and the power of that connected and disconnected and reconnected relationship that seems like it explains the draw and the depth of this much better at least to me.
And so in the rest of the essay is Norman's explanation of eight stages of practice that he's sort of posited, you know that he feels like he's seen and described and noticed in himself and others.
In that situation he really had the opportunity to talk to a lot of people and be on a lot of committees and a lot of meetings, right?
A lot of rubbing shoulders in daily life, you know, going to the Zendo and the dining hall every day.
So in a way it's really not different from what we do, but it's kind of concentrated because you're in it all the time.
So he's coming up with these eight stages, but of course, being a Zen teacher and being Norman, before he tells these to us, he reminds us that they don't actually exist.
Here's Norman again: Of course none of what I'm about to say is true.
There are no stages that occur in a precise sequence, and there are not two communities or individuals that are alike anyway.
So no setting forth of stages or general descriptions of what happens could possibly do justice to the variety of people's experience on the path.
Yet systemic thinking has its virtues.
Systemic thinking has its virtues, and there are great and there are some general tendencies that most of us can notice and recognize.

So here's a little thumbnail sketch from my point of view having just reread this essay of the eight stages, but I'd encourage you to take a look at the Norman's essay itself, either in the book to call it again *When You Greet Me I Bow* or Google it.
This is interesting actually.
If you Google Norman Fischer's "Stages of Monastic Life," Norman Fischer's "Stages of Monastic Life," the top hit I got is a website from the white-robed monks of St.
Benedict with the entire text in there as it appeared in *Windbell* back in the day.
So I assume that's some kind of Catholic monastic order.
So what he said here, as a western Zen person, apparently did land well with at least some true monastics who practice a lifetime of poverty and obedience and renunciation.
We have kind of the soft path, which is in a way easier, in a way a lot harder and more confusing.
It can be in the world and not in the world.

So here are the eight stages in order: the honeymoon is number one, number two disappointment and betrayal, number three exploration of commitment, number four commitment and flight, number five the dry place, number six appreciation and gratitude, number seven love, number eight letting go.
So the first stage, the honeymoon, speaks pretty well for itself, right?
We start things because we're attracted to them, and all new relationships seem to have this exciting early time.
Otherwise, we probably wouldn't stick around, you know, since we're so conditioned to want to do stuff we like.
And who knows how that showed up for you, you know?
Wow, I didn't know there were people in Bellingham who did this stuff.
There's something to the people that do this; they seem really interesting.

Actually, somebody said to me just the other day, a kind of medium-like student said just the other day, "Oh, it's so nice working things out with you Buddhist types—calming down, support for meditation."
Some people are drawn to the ritual, some not so much, as we saw in the many questions about resistance to form that Thales explored with us the other day.
But in these early days, we're hooked, right?
We're psyched; it's cool.
We want to do it.
So the second stage is where it starts to get interesting: disappointment and betrayal.
And Norman really says this is natural and okay and important.
Disappointment and betrayal.
And remember these aren't really discrete stages; you're not only in this and then only in that, right?
They overlap and interweave and come up in different ways.
And probably all eight of these continue to come up our whole lives in different fashions.
But anyway, disappointment: "These people are not that wise after all.
This whole thing may feel a little fake.
What are we doing?
We are not Japanese."
And maybe start to notice the rough edges of sangha organization, and our attention zooms in on these imperfections.
We notice how very imperfect the people are who seemed at first so wise and kind, and somebody misbehaves a little and we are shocked, you know.
I remember feeling some of that in the early days, you know, even way back to Green Gulch, like, "Wow, she's grouchy and complaining about Zazen; she's like a senior student what?"
So maybe I had honeymoon and right away disappointment and betrayal all mixed together back then.
Maybe you do too.
And it's hard too because at first we may have thought that we'd found some ideal—something ideal, companions, ideal practice in the honeymoon.
But later, maybe soon later, damn, you know it all falls short.

But the thing that's practice-wise interesting, important here is we probably don't notice when we're in it how externally focused we're being, as if our happiness and well-being had to do with the website being perfectly updated or so-and-so being just so, you know.
We're not really noticing our inner work yet.
So I think part of the sense of disappointment and betrayal is just where we are on that path, not quite owning our experience and expecting something else to take care of us.
And as we notice that, right there's a real rich field of possibility.
And when people are really in this, it's of course also difficult for the rest of the sangha, but we're committed to each other, and we're committed to practice.
But it can be such a challenge when people really feel unhappy, you know, in the sense of betrayal and disappointment, and they come to us with their suggestions and their concerns and their issues.
And usually these have real truth in them, right?
So that's why they're a little slippery and tricky.
The energy is a little off maybe, but there's truth there.

So it's really interesting if we've been around for a while, this is also part of our practice: with this stage of disappointment and betrayal is how we receive people who are really in it, you know, with kindness and with respect.

They're trying to hear what's actually is valuable and what they say, you know, about some organizational improvement or way we could do things better, but also to hold space for everything being okay as imperfection, you know, and not really being about perfecting things, doing everything right.
So it's a little tricky, and sometimes the person in that stage keeps coming and is dogged, and sometimes they actually just leave, right?
So that's a thing too.
Also hard on us when people leave; we're like, "Oh, what could we have done better, you know?
Could we have been more welcoming?
More understanding?
Kinder?"
Maybe you know, maybe.
Sometimes somebody, I think, just needs to leave.
The third stage is more hopeful: exploration of commitment.
We're getting through the disappointment a little, although it's still present, and we intuit that this song of life is worthwhile even if it's not perfect, even if it's a pain in the butt sometimes.
We commit more to coming to Zazen regularly.
Maybe we start volunteering.
Maybe we start coming to practice discussion and dokusan more often.
Maybe we start showing up presenting, "How can I practice with this?" instead of "Please let's fix this; it's no good."
We're holding both together.
And it's a time of increased stability too in our lives in this stage, which is so encouraging.
And our attention shifts, I think, from rejecting outward as the source of the problem, if there is really a problem here, to looking inward, right.
It's a time of having enough stability to look inward, this exploration of commitment.
And again, these are simplistic, of course; we were doing both all along, but it's more primary.

But this can also be hard because as we increase in commitment and stability, and we increase in our ability to notice what's happening within us—things that Zazen in particular really can reveal, right?
And song of life can really reveal are not always what we are happy to see.
We see our fear and our insecurity more clearly.
We see ourselves being driven to less than great behavior, you know, as our inner demons get a little more space and a little more airtime.
We become stable enough to see how much we're suffering actually.
We can get a little arrogant.
We also can be very apologetic, I think, when we're processing all this stuff.
I thought of our dear departed Dharma sister Nancy Welch; it's a powerful example of some of those dynamics often.
She was so passionate, you know, and so excited, so motivated by practice, pretty loud and flamboyant about it too, really fired up.
And then she'd stumble, and was really good at beating herself up for her stumbles, being so apologetic and also loud.
As you can tell, when I was touching into that stage myself with her, I would get pretty reactive, and we'd yo-yo back and forth together, creating trouble for each other and supporting each other.
Luckily, beneath all of it, there was a deep love that we would remember from time to time.
So this third stage of exploration of commitment can also be kind of dramatic.
In the essay, Norman says of this stage, "This is a really difficult stage, and it can go on for some time.
But it's a really difficult stage, and it can go on for some time.
In fact, it should go on for some time.
If we commit ourselves further in practice too soon, it may well be because we haven't listened to ourselves enough yet."
More work to be done before being too sure we want to commit further, right?
So that's exploration of commitment, that's really a wise name for that, I think.
You do see people move on too quickly, especially in residential centers.
I think that's less true with us.
The fourth stage he posits on the path is the stage of commitment and flight.
Commitment is here again: commitment and flight.
In this stage, our commitment becomes really overt; we're saying out loud one way or the other and demonstrating that we're in, we're committed, we're sticking around.
We've decided this is my path, this is my practice, this is my sangha maybe too.
I'm not going anywhere.
Maybe this takes the form of an outer ritualized step or outer renunciation, like receiving the precepts in Jukai or priest ordination.
We saw the example of Talus the other day with lay entrustment, or a priest going through the lengthy Dharma transmission ceremonies with her teacher to complete the little quadrant there.
And it can be much more subtle.
I always hope there'll be room in the sangha to just sit quietly and just marinate in the Dharma.
You don't have to do all this ritualized stuff.
But in the stage of commitment and flight, there is this decision that happens.
We're not always aware exactly we're making that decision.
I'm not sure I was particularly; I just kind of kept showing up, and then it seemed like I'd made a decision, but a big one, that we're sticking around, this is our life, our life is practice.
And with that commitment, there can be some strong things released.
So he calls it commitment and flight.
